sentences.text: Pentaceratops was a large herbivore that measured between 5.5 and 6 meters in length.
The skull featured a very long frill with two large holes known as parietal fenestrae.
This rectangular frill was decorated with large triangular osteoderms, including up to twelve episquamosals and three epiparietals.
The thick jugal bones did not connect to the squamosals, a trait that might be a unique autapomorphy.
It possessed a short nose horn, two long horns on the forehead, and long horns on the jugal bones.
The name translates to face with five horns, referring to the three typical horns plus two large epiaugal processes on the cheeks.
The skull of specimen AMNH 1624 measures 2.3 meters in length.
Fossils of Pentaceratops were first discovered in 1921.
The initial specimens were collected by Charles Hazelius Sternberg in the San Juan Basin of New Mexico.
Henry Fairfield Osborn named and described the species Pentaceratops sternbergii in 1923.
C. H. Sternberg was the person who found the first Pentaceratops fossils.
Pentaceratops was an herbivore, like all ceratopsians.
It used its sharp beak to bite branches, which were then shredded by its tooth batteries.
Likely food sources included ferns, cycads, and conifers, as flowering plants were geographically limited during its time.
The animal likely exhibited gregarious behavior, similar to most ceratopsians.
Pentaceratops is classified within Ceratopsia, specifically belonging to either the Ceratopsinae or Chasmosaurinae subfamilies.
The genus Pentaceratops was established by Osborn in 1923.
Current classification places Pentaceratops within the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
Osborn originally assigned Pentaceratops to Ceratopsia, within which it belonged to either Ceratopsinae or Chasmosaurinae.
Pentaceratops lived approximately 76 to 73 million years ago, with most fossils found in the Kirtland Formation of the San Juan Basin, New Mexico.
The species lived approximately 76 to 73 million years ago.
Remains have been mostly found in the Kirtland Formation in the San Juan Basin in New Mexico.
Fossils were found in the Fruitland Formation dating to the Campanian, approximately 75 million years ago.
It was common in the Fruitland and Kirtland formations and serves as a guide fossil marking the transition between the Judith and Kirtland vertebrate eras.
In 2016, researchers suggested that Pentaceratops aquilonius might be the same species as Spiclypeus shipporum and considered it a nomen dubium.
Fowler and Freedman Fowler (2020) debated whether Pentaceratops fenestratus is a distinct taxon from Pentaceratops sternbergii.
A new species, Pentaceratops aquilonius, was named by Longrich in 2014.
It is debated whether the largest specimen should remain in Pentaceratops or be classified as the separate genus Titanoceratops.
Identifying specimens as Pentaceratops has sometimes been highly controversial.
